section_1.title: Introduction: The Impossible Counting Puzzle
section_1.content: Introduce the puzzle: Two blocks of mass m and M = 100^n * m sliding on a frictionless surface. We count collisions between the two blocks and the wall. Present the counter-intuitive claim: the total number of collisions equals the first n digits of pi.
section_1.example: Visualize two blocks: a small 'Mouse' block (m=1kg) and a massive 'Elephant' block (M=100kg) heading towards a wall.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
section_2.content: Briefly explain the Elastic Collision framework. We use the Conservation of Momentum and Kinetic Energy to track block velocities. This provides the 'logic' behind why blocks bounce back and forth.
section_2.example: A simple 1D animation showing a ball hitting a wall and reversing velocity, then hitting another ball and transferring energy.

section_3.title: The Geometry of Phase Space
section_3.content: Transition from 1D motion to 2D geometry. By plotting the velocities of the two blocks as coordinates (v1, v2) on a graph, we show that the collision process traces an arc of a circle. This is the 'Aha!' moment where physics becomes geometry.
section_3.example: An animation transforming the 'back-and-forth' collision motion into a bouncing 'ball' inside a circular arc on a Cartesian plane.

section_4.title: Unveiling the Pi Connection
section_4.content: Explain that as the mass ratio M/m increases (powers of 100), the number of collisions is effectively dividing the circumference of a circle by the length of the arc defined by the collision angle, which relates to the arcsin function, leading directly to the digits of pi.
section_4.example: A visual overlay where the trajectory of the 'system state' hits a boundary exactly enough times to map out 3.14...

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Synthesize the concept: Why does a mechanical puzzle generate a transcendental number? Reinforce that symmetry and conservation laws govern not just physics, but the fundamental constants of mathematics.
section_5.example: A final infographic showing: 1 collision = 3, 100 collisions = 31, 10,000 collisions = 314.
